questions.question: Compare Functionalism and Marxism as sociological perspectives.

points.text: Functionalism: consensus-based, society as a system, institutions serve functions, stability is normal. Marxism: conflict-based, society divided by class, institutions serve ruling class, conflict is normal. Functionalism emphasises agreement; Marxism emphasises exploitation. questions.question: Explain how Feminism challenges traditional sociological perspectives.

points.text: Feminism challenges Functionalism (shows institutions like family serve men, not everyone), Marxism (shows class is not the only inequality - gender matters too), and Interactionism (micro-level interactions reflect patriarchal power, not just individual meanings). Feminism has transformed sociology by making gender a central category of analysis, not an afterthought.

questions.question: Evaluate whether Interactionism provides a more valid view of society than Functionalism.

points.text: Interactionism explains how individuals create society through everyday interactions (valid for understanding labelling, identity, roles). Functionalism explains large-scale social patterns (valid for understanding institutional functions). Interactionism strength: accounts for individual experience. points.text: A grade 9 response will: outline each perspective with key concepts and thinkers; evaluate Functionalism (explains order but ignores conflict); evaluate Marxism (explains inequality but overemphasises class); evaluate Feminism (highlights gender but may neglect other inequalities); evaluate Interactionism (explains micro-level but misses macro structures); conclude: no single perspective fully explains society - each reveals different aspects.
